t:
(a) In General.—Subsection (b) of section 121 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 (relating to limitations) is amended by adding at the end the following new paragraph:“(4) Exclusion of gain allocated to nonqualified use.—“(A) In general.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to so much of the gain from the sale or exchange of property as is allocated to periods of nonqualified use.“(B) Gain allocated to periods of nonqualified use.—For purposes of subparagraph (A), gain shall be allocated to periods of nonqualified use based on the ratio which—“(i) the aggregate periods of nonqualified use during the period such property was owned by the taxpayer, bears to“(ii) the period such property was owned by the taxpayer.“(C) Period of nonqualified use.—For purposes of this paragraph—“(i) In general.—The term ‘period of nonqualified use’ means any period (other than the portion of any period preceding January 1, 2009) during which the property is not used as the principal residence of the taxpayer or the taxpayer’s spouse or former spouse.“(ii) Exceptions.—The term ‘period of nonqualified use’ does not include—“(I) any portion of the 5-year period described in subsection (a) which is after the last date that such property is used as the principal residence of the taxpayer or the taxpayer’s spouse,“(II) any period (not to exceed an aggregate period of 10 years) during which the taxpayer or the taxpayer’s spouse is serving on qualified official extended duty (as defined in subsection (d)(9)(C)) described in clause (i), (ii), or (iii) of subsection (d)(9)(A), and“(III) any other period of temporary absence (not to exceed an aggregate period of 2 years) due to change of employment, health conditions, or such other unforeseen circumstances as may be specified by the Secretary.“(D) Coordination with recognition of gain attributable to depreciation.—For purposes of this paragraph—“(i) subparagraph (A) shall be applied after the application of subsection (d)(6), and“(ii) subparagraph (B) shall be applied without regard to any gain to which subsection (d)(6) applies.”. 
    (b) Effective Date.—The amendment made by this section shall apply to sales and exchanges after December 31, 2008.

fable.w: This section amends the tax code to limit the home-sale gain exclusion for periods of nonqualified use; it sets no comment period, hearing, advisory body, outside consultation, or right to sue. The tempting reading is that letting the Secretary specify other unforeseen circumstances is a grant of rulemaking authority. However, the text does not mention regulations or any process involving parties outside the federal government, so it is only a discretionary delegation to a federal official.
fable.s: such other unforeseen circumstances as may be specified by the Secretary

qwen_block.w: This section amends the Internal Revenue Code to define 'nonqualified use' for tax purposes. While it grants the Secretary discretion to specify certain unforeseen circumstances, this is a technical definition for applying a tax exclusion, not a process for public participation or consultation with outside parties before a federal decision. There are no advisory boards, public hearings, comment periods, or consultations with states or the public involved in this provision.
qwen_block.s: any other period of temporary absence (not to exceed an aggregate period of 2 years) due to change of employment, health conditions, or such other unforeseen circumstances as may be specified by the Secretary.

opus.w: This section changes how gain from selling a home is excluded from income, sets out the calculation, and gives an effective date. It calls for no consultation, comment period, hearing, advisory body or right to sue. The only discretionary power is the Secretary's ability to 'specify' extra circumstances. Unlike Example 6, that power is not phrased as authority to act 'by regulation', so it does not clearly require or authorize rulemaking that would bring outside parties in.
opus.s: such other unforeseen circumstances as may be specified by the Secretary
opus.b:
1. **The tempting reading:** The phrase "such other unforeseen circumstances as may be specified by the Secretary" could be read as authority to make rules, as with "may by regulation" in Example 6. That reading fails because the text never mentions regulations or rulemaking. The Secretary of the Treasury could specify these circumstances through internal guidance. No comment period, hearing, advisory body or consultation with outsiders is called for. Everything else in the section is substantive tax arithmetic and an effective date.

2. **Answer:** No, though it is a close call. The answer would flip if the Secretary's power to "specify" circumstances is treated as rulemaking authority.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends the Internal Revenue Code to define 'period of nonqualified use' for tax purposes. While it grants the Secretary discretion to specify 'unforeseen circumstances,' it does not require the Secretary to consult with outside parties, hold public hearings, or engage in rulemaking that mandates public participation. The definition of participation requires interaction with people outside the federal government before a decision is made; here, the Secretary's specification is an internal administrative determination not linked to a required participatory process.
qwen_chat.s: any other period of temporary absence (not to exceed an aggregate period of 2 years) due to change of employment, health conditions, or such other unforeseen circumstances as may be specified by the Secretary.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the phrase "such other unforeseen circumstances as may be specified by the Secretary" implies a rulemaking process that could involve public comment or consultation. However, the definition explicitly states that "requiring rulemaking" is a form of participation, but this clause merely grants the Secretary discretion to define a term within an existing statute. It does not explicitly mandate a public comment period, hearing, or consultation with outside parties. Furthermore, the rest of the section deals with tax calculations and effective dates, which are internal administrative or legislative matters. The key is whether the text *requires* or *recommends* participation. Granting discretion to an agency head is not the same as requiring them to consult with outsiders. Therefore, the answer is No.
